items.name: Ben & Jerry's
clues: Its founders said a business should look after its staff and its community, not just its profits.
Two old school friends opened their first shop in a converted petrol station in Vermont, USA, in 1978.
Ice cream, with big chunks in it and silly flavour names.
It keeps a ‘flavour graveyard’, with a headstone for every flavour it has stopped making.
A huge consumer-goods group bought it in 2000. In 2025 one of the founders quit, saying the company had lost its independence.
Named after its two founders: Mr Cohen and Mr Greenfield, using their first names.

items.name: The Body Shop
clues: One of the first big beauty brands to campaign against testing cosmetics on animals.
Its first shop opened in Brighton, on the south coast of England, in 1976.
Body butters, shower gels, creams and perfume oils.
Its founder became one of Britain’s most famous businesswomen and was made a dame.
Sold to L’Oréal in 2006. After several more owners, its UK business went into administration in 2024.
In American English its name is also a place that repairs cars. Its founder was Anita Roddick.

items.name: Ecosia
clues: Wants to turn something you do dozens of times a day into climate action.
Started in 2009, and is based in Berlin.
Nothing, really: it’s free. It makes its money from adverts, like the big tech companies.
In 2018 its founder gave up the right to sell the company or take its profits out.
Spends most of its profits on planting trees (more than 200 million so far) and has built its own solar plants.
A search engine and an alternative to Google. Its name starts with ‘eco’.

items.name: Lush
clues: Wants to sell beauty products with as little packaging as possible, ideally none at all.
Started in the mid-1990s in Poole, a seaside town in the south of England.
Handmade soap, solid shampoo bars and colourful bath bombs.
In 2021 it closed its Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat accounts, saying social media was bad for mental health.
Says it tests its products on human volunteers and won’t buy from companies that test on animals. One of its founders is called ‘the mother of the bath bomb’.
Its name is a British word for ‘gorgeous’ or ‘lovely’, and it also describes very green, rich grass.

items.name: TOMS
clues: Wanted shopping to feel like giving.
Started in 2006, after its American founder visited Argentina.
Simple canvas slip-on shoes, based on a traditional Argentinian shoe called the alpargata.
Trademarked the phrase ‘One for One’: for every pair you bought, a child in need got a free pair.
Critics said free shoes did little about poverty and could hurt local shoemakers. In 2019 it dropped its famous model and moved to giving grants.
Its short name comes from the word ‘tomorrow’.

items.name: Fairphone
clues: Wants to change how a whole industry makes the thing most people never put down.
Started as a campaign, then became a company in the Netherlands in 2013.
Smartphones built from modules, so you can replace broken parts yourself.
The repair website iFixit gives its phones 10 out of 10 for repairability.
Its 2023 model came with a five-year warranty, far longer than the usual two.
Its name puts an ethical word in front of the thing it sells.
